extracted.intended_audience: current and prospective MFA students, POC creative writers, writing-program faculty and allies
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing and responding to racial inclusivity (or lack thereof) in MFA programs — covering faculty, student body, workshop culture, syllabi, and tactics POC writers can use. Useful for students deciding whether to attend/stay in a program and for faculty/administrators designing programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faculty racial/gender diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: Programs should not be dominated by a single demographic (e.g., “100% white faculties (predominantly male)”). Move away from the default image of The Professor: the straight, white, able-bodied male.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The piece argues that casting institutions differently must start with how faculties are composed — diversify hiring and representation rather than accepting a homogenous professoriate. Acknowledge that white professors can be valuable, but institutions should not be 'eternally, dominantly, lily white.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Student-body racial diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: Graduate programs should have meaningful representation of POC among students rather than isolated individuals (the author reports being one of five in a program of 17, and often the lone 'ethnically marked' person).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lack of peers of color makes students feel like a 'poster child' or 'flag bearer' for ethnicity; absence of representation hinders community-building and future access to networks. Quitting reduces minority representation further (see related criterion about staying).

rubrics_metrics.name: Workshop engagement with race and identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Workshops should explore racial identities and how they impact writing; they should not operate under the assumption that 'race was no longer a major social force.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Junot Díaz is quoted: 'we never explored our racial identities or how they impacted our writing—at all.' Programs should provide instruction and structured conversation on race, sexism, heteronormativity, etc., rather than treating them as irrelevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Curriculum and reading-list diversity
rubrics_metrics.description: Syllabi should not consist mainly of 'dead white guys' or default to narrow canons; reading lists must include writers and theoretical lenses beyond the traditional Western canon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author criticizes curricula dominated by Frankfurt-school figures and canonical poets (Wallace Stevens, O'Haras, etc.) and notes students currently have to craft independent studies to fill gaps. Programs should proactively include feminism, queer theory, disability studies, WOC writers, and other perspectives so students receive a well-rounded education without being forced to supplement it themselves.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid segregated/parallel-only solutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Creating separate, exclusive communities (e.g., specialized multi-genre POC workshops like VONA) is insufficient as the only remedy because it segregates conversations and lets mainstream institutions 'off the hook.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Segregation preserves the status quo by confining race-focused work to 'Summer Minority Camp' instead of integrating it into mainstream programs where white writers and faculty can engage and learn. These workshops are valuable, but not a substitute for institutional change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use status/privilege to pressure institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Those with institutional prestige or visibility should use their power to push universities to balance admissions, design diverse curricula, and expose students to material outside their 'white wheelhouses.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author suggests Junot Díaz (and others in positions of influence) should leverage their profile to catalyze institutional reform rather than only creating alternative spaces. This is framed as a strategic responsibility of privileged actors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don't quit as a default response
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaving a program because it is 'too white' can worsen the problem by further eradicating minority bodies from educational institutions and cutting off access to professional communities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author argues staying can preserve access to publishing/organizing communities and teaching-job pipelines; quitting removes opportunities and representation. This is prescriptive guidance for POC students weighing whether to remain in problematic programs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevent tokenization and othering
rubrics_metrics.description: Programs should avoid implicitly treating POC students as tokens — the 'poster child' or the 'ethnic ranger' — and avoid singling out cultural/linguistic features (e.g., calling attention to Spanish in work as a problem).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tokenization occurs when the burden falls on a few students to represent entire identities. Faculty and peers should not exoticize, question, or otherwise make visible students' language or backgrounds in ways that marginalize them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constructive workshop critique culture
rubrics_metrics.description: Workshop critique should be constructive and craft-focused, not cruel or self-aggrandizing (contrast with 'people shit all over your shitty writing because it makes them feel better').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Toxic workshops where critique is mean-spirited harm development and belonging. Programs should foster critique practices that are rigorous but respectful, supporting writers rather than enacting dominance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Faculty responsibility for diverse syllabi and pedagogy
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual instructors should design syllabi and lead discussions that foreground diverse voices and engage with identities outside their own comfort zones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While not excluding committed white professors, the onus is on instructors to teach materials that expose students to varied traditions and to avoid reproducing hegemonic aesthetic judgments. This complements institutional curriculum reform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide access to professional resources and networks
rubrics_metrics.description: MFA programs should serve as gateways to 'real world' resources — publishing, organizing, and teaching opportunities — not just aesthetic training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author emphasizes that being in a program offers practical benefits (connections, support groups, career pathways) that are especially valuable for writers of color; losing access to these by leaving harms long-term prospects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Students should not have to self-correct curriculum gaps
rubrics_metrics.description: It should not be the student's responsibility to design independent studies to obtain a well-rounded education because the program's standard curriculum is whitewashed or canonized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expecting marginalized students to fill curricular voids reproduces inequality. Programs should proactively build inclusive syllabi and requirements so students are not forced into ad hoc remediation.
